title: Testing a Gene One Patch at a Time
endLine: Mutant patches beside normal neighbours reveal where a gene must act.

scenes.tts: When a broken gene scrambles a tissue, which cells actually need it? Did each cell fail on its own, or because its neighbours failed? If every cell lacks the gene, both causes look identical. To separate them, place mutant cells beside normal neighbours.
scenes.caption: When a broken gene scrambles a tissue, which cells actually need it? Did each cell fail on its own, or because its neighbours failed? If every cell lacks the gene, both causes look identical. To separate them, place mutant cells beside normal neighbours.
scenes.visual: Full-frame schematic hexagonal cell sheet in calm teal, gently pulsing. Within the first 3 seconds, every cell flips to amber and small surface polarity arrows scramble at once while the opening question appears. A spotlight sweeps between one amber cell and its surrounding amber neighbours, then halves the sheet into amber mutant cells touching teal normal cells.
scenes.narration: When a broken gene scrambles a tissue, which cells actually need it? Did each cell fail on its own, or because its neighbours failed? If every cell lacks the gene, both causes look identical. To separate them, place mutant cells beside normal neighbours.

scenes.visual: The schematic cell sheet continues its slow ambient drift behind a clean high-contrast title overlay: "Testing a Gene One Patch at a Time".

scenes.tts: That is genetic mosaic analysis: making one tissue of two genetic kinds. Inside an otherwise normal animal, you mutate one cell and permanently mark it. Every descendant inherits both changes, forming a clone: a visible mutant patch amid normal cells.
scenes.caption: That is genetic mosaic analysis: making one tissue of two genetic kinds. Inside an otherwise normal animal, you mutate one cell and permanently mark it. Every descendant inherits both changes, forming a clone: a visible mutant patch amid normal cells.
scenes.visual: The same schematic teal cell sheet resets to all normal cells. One central cell flashes bright magenta (mutant plus permanent mark) and divides step by step—one cell into two, four, eight, sixteen—pushing into a cohesive magenta patch surrounded by normal teal cells. Labels (size 28+): "Mutant clone (schematic)" and "Normal neighbours".
scenes.narration: That is genetic mosaic analysis: making one tissue of two genetic kinds. Inside an otherwise normal animal, you mutate one cell and permanently mark it. Every descendant inherits both changes, forming a clone: a visible mutant patch amid normal cells.

scenes.tts: Now watch the border where mutant cells touch normal neighbours. If a gene acts inside the cell, only the patch changes. If it signals between cells, normal neighbours can change too, or supply what the patch lacks.
scenes.caption: Now watch the border where mutant cells touch normal neighbours. If a gene acts inside the cell, only the patch changes. If it signals between cells, normal neighbours can change too, or supply what the patch lacks.
scenes.visual: Camera zooms smoothly onto the border between the magenta mutant clone and teal normal cells; a glowing dashed line traces the border (schematic). First, internal sparks shift only the magenta cells ("Inside the cell"). Next, arrows cross the border—first shifting adjacent teal neighbours, then flowing inward from teal to supply what the magenta border cells lack ("Between cells").
scenes.narration: Now watch the border where mutant cells touch normal neighbours. If a gene acts inside the cell, only the patch changes. If it signals between cells, normal neighbours can change too, or supply what the patch lacks.

scenes.tts: On a fly sheet, touching cells talk by contact, and each becomes neural or epidermis, the outer skin. Delta is the signal saying, not you: do not turn neural. Notch is the receptor that hears it. Patches lacking Notch cannot hear, so they turn neural. Predict: does a patch lacking Delta turn neural?
scenes.caption: On a fly sheet, touching cells talk by contact, and each becomes neural or epidermis, the outer skin. Delta is the signal saying, "not you: do not turn neural." Notch is the receptor that hears it. Patches lacking Notch cannot hear, so they turn neural. Predict: does a patch lacking Delta turn neural?
scenes.visual: Two labels appear first, as spoken: gold "Neural" and flat teal "Epidermis (outer skin)". On the same schematic cell sheet, small outward pegs ("Delta: signal") and inward cups ("Notch: receptor") appear along touching walls. In a magenta patch lacking Notch cups, incoming Delta pegs from teal neighbours bounce off and the patch cells brighten gold ("Neural"). The patch resets: Notch cups return, Delta pegs vanish from the magenta patch while staying intact on normal teal neighbours. Question banner appears: "Patch lacks Delta: does it turn neural?"
scenes.narration: On a fly sheet, touching cells talk by contact, and each becomes neural or epidermis, the outer skin. Delta is the signal saying, "not you: do not turn neural." Notch is the receptor that hears it. Patches lacking Notch cannot hear, so they turn neural. Predict: does a patch lacking Delta turn neural?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause (4.5 s). The question "Patch lacks Delta: does it turn neural?" remains on screen while schematic Delta pegs on the normal teal neighbours gently pulse against the intact Notch cups on the magenta patch cells.

scenes.tts: Patches lacking Delta do not turn neural on their own. Losing Delta removes only what a cell sends, not what it hears. They still have Notch, so normal neighbours' Delta still tells them, not you. So a mosaic separates sending a signal from hearing it.
scenes.caption: Patches lacking Delta do not turn neural on their own. Losing Delta removes only what a cell sends, not what it hears. They still have Notch, so normal neighbours' Delta still tells them, "not you." So a mosaic separates sending a signal from hearing it.
scenes.visual: Delta pegs from the normal teal neighbours dock into the Notch cups of the magenta cells mutant for Delta; a calm ripple labelled "Not you" spreads inward and the patch cells stay un-gold: they do not turn neural on their own (schematic). Empty spaces on the magenta walls highlight that only outgoing Delta is missing. Closing labels: "Sending: lost" and "Hearing: intact".
scenes.narration: Patches lacking Delta do not turn neural on their own. Losing Delta removes only what a cell sends, not what it hears. They still have Notch, so normal neighbours' Delta still tells them, "not you." So a mosaic separates sending a signal from hearing it.

scenes.tts: Two traps can mislead. Pulse labels like E D U dilute as cells divide, so marks must be permanent. Marking two neighbouring cells at once can mimic one clone. So controls mark sparsely and count close pairs in short-term samples. They also check the mark stays off without the inducer, its trigger.
scenes.caption: Two traps can mislead. Pulse labels like EdU dilute as cells divide, so marks must be permanent. Marking two neighbouring cells at once can mimic one clone. So controls mark sparsely and count close pairs in short-term samples. They also check the mark stays off without the inducer, its trigger.
scenes.visual: Pulling back on the same schematic sheet: first, a pale blue pulse tint ("EdU") divides and fades to near-invisible over several divisions (schematic), replaced by a crisp permanent magenta mark. Next, dense induction lights two adjacent cells whose growing clones fuse into one deceptive patch ("Two clones merged"). A schematic "Sparse" control reduces marks to well-separated single cells with a short-term spacing check, alongside a dark control sheet labelled "No inducer (trigger): mark off".
scenes.narration: Two traps can mislead. Pulse labels like EdU dilute as cells divide, so marks must be permanent. Marking two neighbouring cells at once can mimic one clone. So controls mark sparsely and count close pairs in short-term samples. They also check the mark stays off without the inducer, its trigger.

scenes.tts: Mosaics also unlocked how tissues coordinate. Fly wing hairs all point toward the tip. In 1987, Charles Vinson and Paul Adler made patches lacking frizzled in normal wings. Normal cells on the tip side grew misdirected hairs; those on the other side did not. So frizzled's effect reached beyond the mutant cells.
scenes.caption: Mosaics also unlocked how tissues coordinate. Fly wing hairs all point toward the tip. In 1987, Charles Vinson and Paul Adler made patches lacking frizzled in normal wings. Normal cells on the tip side grew misdirected hairs; those on the other side did not. So frizzled's effect reached beyond the mutant cells.
scenes.visual: On the same schematic cell sheet, every cell grows a crisp wing hair pointing right toward "Wing tip". A central magenta patch of cells lacking frizzled appears; normal teal cells on the tip side (right of the patch) swivel into misdirected hairs, while normal cells on the opposite side stay neatly aligned. Label: "Vinson & Adler, 1987 (schematic)".
scenes.narration: Mosaics also unlocked how tissues coordinate. Fly wing hairs all point toward the tip. In 1987, Charles Vinson and Paul Adler made patches lacking frizzled in normal wings. Normal cells on the tip side grew misdirected hairs; those on the other side did not. So frizzled's effect reached beyond the mutant cells.

scenes.tts: Those Notch and Delta patches came from Pascal Heitzler and Pat Simpson in 1991. They also varied Notch activity. A normal cell beside cells with less Notch activity became epidermis; beside more, a neural precursor. Fate followed how a cell's Notch activity compared with its neighbours'.
scenes.caption: Those Notch and Delta patches came from Pascal Heitzler and Pat Simpson in 1991. They also varied Notch activity. A normal cell beside cells with less Notch activity became epidermis; beside more, a neural precursor. Fate followed how a cell's Notch activity compared with its neighbours'.
scenes.visual: The schematic sheet shifts to two side-by-side border comparisons ("Heitzler & Simpson, 1991"): a normal teal cell touching dim low-Notch neighbours flattens into "Epidermis", while an identical normal teal cell touching bright high-Notch neighbours lights up gold as a "Neural precursor". A schematic comparison bar highlights relative Notch level across each border.
scenes.narration: Those Notch and Delta patches came from Pascal Heitzler and Pat Simpson in 1991. They also varied Notch activity. A normal cell beside cells with less Notch activity became epidermis; beside more, a neural precursor. Fate followed how a cell's Notch activity compared with its neighbours'.

scenes.tts: Mosaics even reach single neurons. M A R C M labels one or a few neurons in an unlabelled brain, making only those mutant. In 2000, Tzumin Lee, Liqun Luo and colleagues tested fly brain cells called gamma neurons. Each needed the steroid receptor E c R B one inside itself to remodel at metamorphosis. Normal surroundings pinpoint where a gene must act.
scenes.caption: Mosaics even reach single neurons. MARCM labels one or a few neurons in an unlabelled brain, making only those mutant. In 2000, Tzumin Lee, Liqun Luo and colleagues tested fly brain cells called gamma neurons. Each needed the steroid receptor EcR-B1 inside itself to remodel at metamorphosis. Normal surroundings pinpoint where a gene must act.
scenes.visual: The cell sheet dissolves into a dark schematic fly brain outline filled with faint unlabelled neurons; one gamma neuron lights up bright magenta via MARCM ("Lee, Luo et al., 2000"). As metamorphosis sweeps across, faint normal neighbours prune back their branches while the single magenta EcR-B1-mutant neuron keeps its unpruned branches intact inside the normal brain (schematic).
scenes.narration: Mosaics even reach single neurons. MARCM labels one or a few neurons in an unlabelled brain, making only those mutant.
